cards.front: What do generics add beyond interfaces for reuse?
cards.back: Type parameters: code works with some unspecified type while the compiler still checks it
cards.extra: An interface fixes the type to that interface. A generic method fixes nothing, and each caller chooses — with full compile-time checking at the call site.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static  T first(java.util.List xs) { return xs.get(0); }
  public static void main(String[] a) { System.out.println(first(java.util.Arrays.asList("a")) + " " + first(java.util.Arrays.asList(2))); }
}

cards.front: What does a generic container give you that a pre-SE5 one did not?
cards.back: The compiler rejects the wrong element type, and casts disappear from your code
cards.extra: Before generics everything was Object, so an Apple could enter a list of Oranges and only fail on retrieval. Now the error is at the insertion site.
cards.example:
java.util.List xs = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
xs.add("a");
String s = xs.get(0); // no cast needed
// xs.add(1); // would not compile: wrong element type

cards.back: By erasure: type parameters are removed and replaced by their bounds (or Object)
cards.extra: One class file serves every instantiation, which is why old code and new code interoperate. C++ instead generates a separate class per type.
cards.example:
java.util.List ss = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
java.util.List ns = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
System.out.println(ss.getClass() == ns.getClass()); // true: both are ArrayList after erasure

cards.back: Anything needing the type at runtime: new T(), instanceof T, T[], T.class
cards.extra: The type only exists to the compiler. That is why generic code passes a Class token or a factory when it needs to construct elements.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static  java.util.List empty() {
    // new T(), o instanceof T, new T[1] and T.class are illegal: erasure removes T
    return new java.util.ArrayList<>();
  }
}

cards.front: Can a primitive be a type argument?
cards.back: No — use the wrapper, and autoboxing hides the difference
cards.extra: List<int> is illegal; List<Integer> works. Erasure is the reason: there is no primitive type left at runtime.
cards.example:
java.util.List xs = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
xs.add(3); // int autoboxed to Integer; List would not compile
System.out.println(xs.get(0));

cards.front: What is a bounded type parameter for?
cards.back: Guaranteeing capabilities: <T extends Number> lets the body call Number methods
cards.extra: Without a bound, the compiler treats T as Object and allows only Object's methods. The bound is also what erasure substitutes.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static  double half(T n) { return n.doubleValue() / 2; }
  public static void main(String[] a) { System.out.println(half(5) + " " + half(3.5)); }
}

cards.front: What does a wildcard such as ? extends Shape express?
cards.back: "Some subtype of Shape, unknown" — read from it, but you cannot add to it safely
cards.extra: List<? extends Shape> accepts a List of Circles; you can read Shapes out, but adding is refused because the exact element type is unknown.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static class Shape {}
  static class Circle extends Shape {}
  static void read(java.util.List xs) { Shape s = xs.get(0); } // xs.add(new Circle()) will not compile
  public static void main(String[] a) { read(java.util.Arrays.asList(new Circle())); }
}
